Analyzing Diagnostic Tests without a Gold Standard

ClinicoPath Development Team

2026-11-08

Source: vignettes/12-nogoldstandard.Rmd
12-nogoldstandard.Rmd

Introduction

Evaluating a diagnostic test usually needs a reference (“gold”) standard that tells us who truly has the disease. Often no such reference exists, or it is too invasive, costly or unethical to apply to everyone. The nogoldstandard analysis estimates how several imperfect tests behave from the patterns of agreement and disagreement among them, without a reference test.

This vignette shows how to:

  1. fit a two-class latent class model and read its class proportion and response probabilities,
  2. obtain bootstrap confidence intervals,
  3. compare the latent-model results with simple reference rules,
  4. check, and understand the limits of checking, the conditional-independence assumption.

Every code chunk below is executed when the vignette is built.

Methods Overview

The analysis offers five methods.

  1. Latent class analysis (latent_class, the default): a two-class model in which the tests are assumed to err independently within each class (conditional independence). Fitted by maximum likelihood.
  2. Penalized EM (bayesian): the same two-class model, fitted with fixed priors. Prevalence uses a uniform Beta(1, 1) prior; sensitivity and specificity each use a Beta(2, 1) prior, which adds one pseudo true-positive and one pseudo true-negative result to every test and pulls both estimates upward. The result is a penalized-likelihood (MAP) point estimate, not a posterior sample, and the priors cannot be changed.
  3. Composite reference (composite): a patient is reference-positive when more than half of the tests are positive (a tie counts as negative). Each evaluated test votes on the reference it is then compared with (incorporation bias), so its agreement can be distorted in either direction.
  4. All tests positive (all_positive): reference-positive only when every test is positive.
  5. Any test positive (any_positive): reference-positive when at least one test is positive.

The three rule methods report agreement of each test with a rule built from the same tests. That is not diagnostic accuracy.

The latent methods need at least three tests; the analysis refuses two.

Example Data

Four imperfect tests on 200 patients. In this simulation the true status is known, so we can compare the estimates with the truth; in practice it is not.

library(meddecide)

set.seed(123)
n <- 200
true_status <- rbinom(n, 1, 0.3)  # 30% prevalence

simulate_test <- function(sens, spec) {
  ifelse(true_status == 1, rbinom(n, 1, sens), rbinom(n, 1, 1 - spec))
}
to_factor <- function(x) factor(ifelse(x == 1, "pos", "neg"), levels = c("neg", "pos"))

data <- data.frame(
  caseID = 1:n,
  test1 = to_factor(simulate_test(0.90, 0.90)),
  test2 = to_factor(simulate_test(0.75, 0.95)),
  test3 = to_factor(simulate_test(0.85, 0.85)),
  test4 = to_factor(simulate_test(0.70, 0.95))
)
head(data)
#>   caseID test1 test2 test3 test4
#> 1      1   pos   neg   pos   neg
#> 2      2   neg   pos   pos   pos
#> 3      3   pos   neg   neg   neg
#> 4      4   pos   pos   neg   pos
#> 5      5   pos   pos   pos   pos
#> 6      6   neg   pos   pos   neg

Running the Analysis

In R every test slot and every positive-level argument must be supplied. Unused slots are passed as NULL (a positive level is a required argument of the R function even when its test is not used).

result <- nogoldstandard(
  data = data,
  test1 = "test1", test1Positive = "pos",
  test2 = "test2", test2Positive = "pos",
  test3 = "test3", test3Positive = "pos",
  test4 = "test4", test4Positive = "pos",
  test5 = NULL, test5Positive = NULL,
  method = "latent_class"
)

result$prevalence$asDF
#>      estimate ci_lower ci_upper
#> "1" 0.2862007       NA       NA
result$test_metrics$asDF[, c("test", "sensitivity", "specificity", "ppv", "npv")]
#>          test sensitivity specificity       ppv       npv
#> "test1" test1   0.9468650   0.9103297 0.8089356 0.9771319
#> "test2" test2   0.6231854   0.9416588 0.8107095 0.8617377
#> "test3" test3   0.8209333   0.8878560 0.7458784 0.9251839
#> "test4" test4   0.6320051   0.9311856 0.7864361 0.8632203

Results tables are read with $asDF, which is a field, not a function: write result$prevalence$asDF, not result$prevalence$asDF().

The output contains:

  1. the fitted proportion of the high-positive latent class,
  2. for each test, the probability of a positive result in the high-positive class and of a negative result in the other class, with predictive values,
  3. model-fit statistics and a conditional-independence check (bivariate residuals),
  4. the test agreement table and plot.

Bootstrap Confidence Intervals

With bootstrap = TRUE the analysis resamples patients with replacement, refits the selected method on each resample, and reports percentile intervals. The point estimates do not change; only intervals are added. seed makes the intervals reproducible. nboot must be at least 100; use 1000 or more for reported results (100 keeps this vignette fast).

result_ci <- nogoldstandard(
  data = data,
  test1 = "test1", test1Positive = "pos",
  test2 = "test2", test2Positive = "pos",
  test3 = "test3", test3Positive = "pos",
  test4 = "test4", test4Positive = "pos",
  test5 = NULL, test5Positive = NULL,
  method = "latent_class",
  bootstrap = TRUE, nboot = 100, alpha = 0.05, seed = 42
)
result_ci$prevalence$asDF
#>      estimate  ci_lower  ci_upper
#> "1" 0.2862007 0.2183321 0.3505935

Percentile intervals can be too narrow with weak identification, estimates at 0% or 100%, or small samples; nominal coverage is not guaranteed. Rows are resampled as independent patients, so the intervals do not account for clustering (several specimens from one patient).

Comparing Methods 

methods <- c("latent_class", "bayesian", "composite", "all_positive", "any_positive")
results <- lapply(methods, function(m) {
  nogoldstandard(
    data = data,
    test1 = "test1", test1Positive = "pos",
    test2 = "test2", test2Positive = "pos",
    test3 = "test3", test3Positive = "pos",
    test4 = "test4", test4Positive = "pos",
    test5 = NULL, test5Positive = NULL,
    method = m
  )
})
names(results) <- methods

sapply(results, function(x) x$prevalence$asDF$estimate[1])
#> latent_class     bayesian    composite all_positive any_positive 
#>    0.2862007    0.2846912    0.2150000    0.0900000    0.5000000

The methods estimate different quantities:

  • Latent class analysis and penalized EM estimate the proportion of the high-positive latent class. Penalized EM is pulled toward higher sensitivity and specificity by its fixed priors; with a large sample the two agree closely.
  • All tests positive gives the smallest rule-positive proportion and any test positive the largest, by construction.
  • Composite is a majority vote that includes the evaluated test.

Interpreting Results

Class proportion, not automatically prevalence

Latent classes are unlabeled. The analysis names the class whose tests are, on average, more often positive the “high-positive” class. Calling it the diseased class, its proportion the prevalence, and the response probabilities sensitivity and specificity requires the substantive assumption that positive results are more common in diseased patients for most tests. If a positive level is selected the wrong way round, a test can come out below chance (sensitivity plus specificity below 1), and the analysis warns about it.

For the rule methods the “prevalence” is the proportion meeting the rule, and sensitivity and specificity are agreement with that rule.

Conditional independence

The latent model assumes the tests err independently within each class. Two tests that share a mechanism (the same target, the same reader, the same specimen) can violate this assumption and bias the estimates; sharing a mechanism alone does not prove conditional dependence.

  • Four or five tests: the bivariate-residual table compares each observed pairwise table with the one the fitted model implies. A residual above 3.84 is descriptive evidence against conditional independence, and the analysis then raises a warning. The flagged pair is not necessarily the dependent pair: the latent classes can absorb dependence between two tests so that the misfit appears elsewhere. Penalized EM shows the same table, computed from the unpenalized fit of the same model.
  • Three tests: the two-class model has 7 parameters for 7 free cell frequencies, so it usually reproduces the observed table exactly. Dependence cannot be detected from the data, the residuals read “Not assessable”, and the analysis warns that conditional independence cannot be checked. A fourth test creates residual degrees of freedom and permits some model checks; it does not guarantee detection of dependence or identify the responsible test pair.

The analysis does not fit dependence models (direct test-to-test associations, more than two classes, or random-effects latent class models).

Missing data

The analysis is complete-case: a patient with a missing result on any selected test is excluded from every estimate, and the number of analysed cases out of the total is reported. If results are not missing completely at random, the estimates can be biased.

Recommendations for Practice

  1. Use latent class analysis as the primary method, with at least four tests when you can, and read its conditional-independence check before interpreting the response probabilities as accuracy.
  2. Treat penalized EM as a stabilized version of the same model for small samples, not as a way to supply prior knowledge; its priors are fixed.
  3. Report the rule methods as agreement, not as accuracy.
  4. Report bootstrap intervals (1000 or more resamples) with the seed.
  5. Validate against external data, follow-up, or a reference test on a subset of patients where possible.

References

  1. Hui SL, Walter SD. Estimating the error rates of diagnostic tests. Biometrics. 1980;36(1):167-171.

  2. Joseph L, Gyorkos TW, Coupal L. Bayesian estimation of disease prevalence and the parameters of diagnostic tests in the absence of a gold standard. Am J Epidemiol. 1995;141(3):263-272.

  3. Albert PS, Dodd LE. A cautionary note on the robustness of latent class models for estimating diagnostic error without a gold standard. Biometrics. 2004;60(2):427-435.

  4. Collins J, Huynh M. Estimation of diagnostic test accuracy without full verification: a review of latent class methods. Stat Med. 2014;33(24):4141-4169.

  5. Dendukuri N, Joseph L. Bayesian approaches to modeling the conditional dependence between multiple diagnostic tests. Biometrics. 2001;57(1):158-167.
